40666:
Job is set in a world that feels older than Moses. There is no temple, no Torah, no Israel. Job offers sacrifices himself as head of his household (Job 1:5), measures wealth in flocks and servants, and lives to 140 (Job 42:16), like the patriarchs. This 'once upon a time' setting is deliberate: it lifts the story out of any one moment in Israel's history so that it can speak to all of them.

The book belongs to a wider ancient conversation. Mesopotamian texts such as *Ludlul bel nemeqi* and the *Babylonian Theodicy* also describe a pious man struck down by sickness and social ruin. What makes Job different is its shape: a prose folk tale wraps around a long poetic debate (Job 3-42:6), and the poetry refuses the happy resolution until God himself speaks. In the ancient parallels the gods restore the sufferer; in Job the deeper issue is whether a human being will love God 'for nothing' (Job 1:9).

The central debate is a clash between an honest sufferer and a theory. Job's friends hold a version of retribution theology: God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked in this life, so great suffering must mean hidden sin (Job 4:7-8; Job 8:3-6). That idea was not foolish; it is a fair summary of many proverbs and of the covenant blessings and curses (Deut 28). The problem is that they make a general truth into a rule that explains every case. Job knows he is innocent, and the reader knows it too, because God himself said so (Job 1:8).

The Hebrew of the poetry is among the hardest in the Bible, with more rare words than any other book. Translations differ widely in places, and the Greek translation is about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew. Readers should expect footnotes and should hold some verses loosely.
40668: The Hebrew is *ha-satan*, 'the accuser' or 'the adversary', with the definite article, more like a job title than a personal name. He appears among the 'sons of God' (heavenly beings) presenting themselves before the LORD, like officials at a royal court, and acts as a kind of prosecutor who questions Job's motives. Later Jewish and Christian tradition identified him with the devil; the book itself keeps the focus on God's sovereignty.
40670: Job's loss is not only pain but disgrace. He once sat at the city gate as a respected elder (Job 29:7-10); now young men mock him and spit at him (Job 30:1-10). In an honour culture, suffering looked like public evidence of God's disfavour, which is why the friends' explanation stung so badly.
40672: The friends tear their robes, throw dust on their heads and sit with Job on the ground for seven days in silence (the length of a funeral mourning). This was right; their mistake began when they started explaining.
40674: Job speaks like a man filing a legal case. He wants an umpire or arbiter between himself and God (Job 9:33), a witness in heaven (Job 16:19), a redeemer to stand up for him (Job 19:25), and he signs his final oath of innocence like a legal document: 'here is my signature' (Job 31:35).
40676: God's second speech points to two great creatures. Behemoth is often linked with the hippopotamus and Leviathan with the crocodile, but both also carry the colour of ancient sea-and-chaos monsters (compare Ugaritic Lotan). God's point is that what humans cannot tame, he made and governs.
40678: Job is not an Israelite, yet he 'fears God and turns away from evil' (Job 1:1). Like Melchizedek or Jethro, he shows that the God of Israel is known and honoured beyond Israel, and that wisdom's core is reverence for God.
40679:
Jewish tradition has treated Job with both admiration and argument. The Talmud preserves a discussion of when Job lived, ranging from the time of the patriarchs to the return from exile, and the striking view of Resh Lakish that Job 'never existed but was a parable' (Bava Batra 15a); either way, the rabbis took its question seriously. Some rabbis praised Job as a God-fearer even greater than Abraham; others criticised his bitter words against heaven. Job is one of the few books that may be studied on Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the temple's destruction, because its subject is grief.

Read within Israel's covenant story, Job tests a misunderstanding of the covenant rather than the covenant itself. Deuteronomy promised blessing for faithfulness and curse for unfaithfulness (Deut 28), and many Israelites heard that as a strict formula. Job shows that the relationship with God is deeper than a contract of rewards: Job keeps addressing God, even accusingly, when God seems absent, and that persistent speaking-to-God is itself loyalty. God's verdict at the end is startling: Job, who protested, 'spoke what is right' about God, while the friends, who defended God with neat theology, did not (Job 42:7-8).

Medieval Jewish thinkers made Job a test case for providence. Saadia Gaon read it as a book about trials that refine; Maimonides (*Guide for the Perplexed* 3.22-23) read Job as moving from moral uprightness to true knowledge of God, after which his suffering no longer overwhelms him. The Aramaic Targum of Job found among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QtgJob) shows the book was studied and translated by Jews before the time of Jesus.
40681: The accuser asks whether Job serves God 'for nothing'. Job loses wealth, children and health, yet blesses God.
40682: Silence, then a curse on birth
40683: Three friends sit with him seven days. Then Job breaks the silence by cursing the day he was born.
40685: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar argue in three rounds that suffering means sin and urge Job to repent. Job insists on his innocence.
40687: Job longs for an arbiter, a heavenly witness and a living redeemer, and finally swears an oath of innocence demanding God answer.
40688: A poem says humans can mine silver but cannot dig up wisdom; only God knows its place. Elihu then argues that suffering can be God's discipline.
40690: God asks Job a torrent of questions about creation, from the sea's boundaries to the wild animals, and the monsters Behemoth and Leviathan.
40692: Job says he had heard of God but now sees him, and withdraws his case.
40694: God says the friends did not speak rightly as Job did; Job prays for them and his fortunes are restored double.
40715: Whole, complete, of integrity; not sinless but undivided in loyalty to God. The related word *tummah*, 'integrity', is what Job refuses to let go of.
40717: Freely, without payment or reason. The accuser asks whether Job fears God 'for nothing'; later God says Job was ruined 'without reason'. The same word frames the whole test.
40718: The next of kin who stands up for a family member, buys back land, frees a relative or avenges blood. Job is sure such a defender lives and will stand on the earth.
40719: Skill in living rightly in God's world. Job 28 insists that the deepest wisdom is not a technique humans can mine but a gift tied to the fear of the Lord.
40721: 'The accuser', a title for a member of the heavenly court who challenges Job's motives.
40722: Proverbs teaches the general pattern that wisdom brings life; Job tests the hard cases where the pattern seems to fail. Both end at the same place: the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
40723: Ecclesiastes shares Job's honesty about injustice under the sun and death that levels everyone.
40724: Job's protest prayers belong to the same family as the lament psalms, which also accuse God of absence and still speak to him.
40725: Job's patriarchal setting, long life and household sacrifices recall Abraham, another God-fearer tested by God.
40726: James holds up Job as an example of endurance and of the Lord's compassion and mercy at the end.
40727: Paul quotes Job's wording when praising God whom no one can put in debt.
40728: Christians have heard in Job's longing for an arbiter who could 'lay his hand on us both' (Job 9:33) and a living redeemer (Job 19:25) an ache that the New Testament sees answered in Jesus, the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Tim 2:5). Jesus also embodies the innocent sufferer whom observers assume is cursed by God, and he prays a lament from the cross (Matt 27:46). Jewish readers do not read Job messianically; they see in the go'el God himself or a heavenly advocate. Both traditions agree that Job dismantles the idea that suffering always reveals the sufferer's guilt, something Jesus himself rejects (John 9:1-3).
40729: Quoting Job's friends as God's word
40730: Because every verse of Job is Scripture, a line such as 'whoever was innocent ever perished?' (Job 4:7) or 'God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves' (Job 11:6) can be quoted on its own as a true statement about how God works.
40731: The friends' speeches are inspired records of what they said, but God's final verdict is that they 'have not spoken of me what is right' (Job 42:7). Their individual sentences often sound like Proverbs; the error is applying a general pattern as a rule to Job's case. Commentators across traditions, from Carol Newsom to John Walton, read the speeches as voices in a debate that the book as a whole evaluates.
40732: Evangelical scholars such as Walton and Tremper Longman agree with this. They add that many of the friends' statements are true in general (Paul even quotes Eliphaz in 1 Cor 3:19 from Job 5:13), so the issue is not that every word is false but that the friends used truth carelessly and without love.
40733: Pastors and friends who quote the friends to sufferers repeat the very mistake God condemned. The book trains readers to ask who is speaking and how the book judges them.
40734: Job as a story about the devil's power
40735: Job shows that Satan causes our sickness and losses, so the key response is spiritual warfare against the enemy.
40736: In Job, the adversary can do nothing without God's permission and disappears from the story after chapter 2. Job never learns about the heavenly scene, and God's speeches never mention the satan. The book's focus is Job's relationship with God, not a battle with the devil.
40737: Many evangelical teachers rightly note that Scripture elsewhere does describe a real enemy (1 Pet 5:8) and that Job 1-2 shows evil is limited by God. Both sides agree the heavenly prologue reassures readers that suffering is not outside God's rule, even when we cannot see the reason.
40738: Reading Job mainly as demonology can distract from its real comfort: that one may bring raw grief and protest straight to God and still be counted faithful.
40739: For Israelites who had lost land, temple and king, Job gave permission to grieve honestly, warned against glib explanations, and pointed them to a God who is free, wise and present even when silent.
40740: Job teaches how to sit with sufferers before speaking, that lament is a form of faith rather than its failure, and that some suffering has no explanation we will be given. It also rebukes any prosperity message that treats health and wealth as proof of God's favour.
40741: Israel's songbook and prayer book: 150 poems, gathered into five books, that teach God's people to praise, complain, confess, trust and wait for his King.
40743: David, the shepherd-king and musician (1 Sam 16:23), heads the list, with 73 psalms headed 'of David'. Others are linked to Asaph and the sons of Korah (temple singers appointed in Chronicles), Solomon, Moses, Heman and Ethan. About fifty are anonymous. Editors and temple singers later arranged the whole collection.
40744: Mostly from the superscriptions, the short headings above many psalms (in Hebrew Bibles they are counted as verse 1). Some give historical settings, such as Ps 51 after David's sin with Bathsheba or Ps 3 when he fled from Absalom. The Hebrew *le-david* can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to' David, so scholars debate how much the headings claim. The New Testament cites several psalms as David's words (Acts 2:25-31; Mark 12:36).
40746: 2 Sam 1:19-27 (David's lament for Saul and Jonathan)
40747: Jerusalem, especially the temple, and in exile
40748: Most psalms assume Zion and temple worship; some were written in exile (Ps 137 by the rivers of Babylon). The collection was finalised in Jerusalem in the second-temple period.
40749: Israel at worship, gathered and alone
40750: Jerusalem temple, homes, pilgrim roads, exile and later the synagogue
40751: Psalms were sung at festivals, on pilgrimage (Ps 120-134), at sacrifices of thanksgiving, in times of national disaster and in private prayer. As a finished book, the Psalter also became a guide to meditation, opened by Ps 1, which blesses the person who meditates on the LORD's instruction day and night.
40752: Not a narrative, but the psalms span from the Davidic monarchy (and Ps 90, traditionally Mosaic) to the exile and return.
40753: David makes Jerusalem his capital and brings the ark there (2 Sam 6).
40754: Solomon's temple is built; Chronicles links temple singing to Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chr 25:1).
40755: Babylon destroys the temple and the Davidic kingship ends, the crisis voiced in Ps 89 and Ps 137.
40756: The second temple is dedicated; post-exilic psalms of praise and the closing Hallelujahs take shape.
40757: The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a) at Qumran shows a differently ordered collection still in use alongside the familiar one (dating approximate).
40758:
The Psalms grew over about six centuries. Individual poems were written for real moments: a king going to war (Ps 20), a sick person recovering (Ps 30), the nation after defeat (Ps 44), pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem (Ps 122). Smaller collections came first, such as the psalms of Asaph (Ps 73-83), the sons of Korah (Ps 42-49; Ps 84-88) and the Songs of Ascents (Ps 120-134). A note at Ps 72:20, 'the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended', is a fossil from an earlier stage when a David collection closed there.

The finished Psalter is divided into five books, each ending with a doxology, a short burst of praise ending in 'Amen' (Ps 41:13; Ps 72:18-19; Ps 89:52; Ps 106:48), with Ps 150 as the grand finale. Many see a deliberate parallel with the five books of Moses. Gerald Wilson argued in 1985 that the arrangement tells a story: Books I-II celebrate David's kingship, Book III ends with the anguished cry of Ps 89 that God has renounced his covenant with David, and Book IV answers with Moses (Ps 90) and the cry 'The LORD reigns!' (Ps 93; Ps 96-99). Not all scholars accept so detailed a storyline, but most now read the Psalter as a shaped book, not a random hymnal.

Hermann Gunkel (early 20th century) sorted psalms by type: hymns of praise, individual and community laments, thanksgivings, royal psalms, wisdom psalms and others. Laments are the single largest group, which surprises many modern worshippers. Walter Brueggemann later described the movement of the Psalms as orientation (life makes sense), disorientation (life falls apart) and new orientation (surprised by God's rescue).

Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds; it 'rhymes' ideas. The basic unit is parallelism: a second line echoes, sharpens, contrasts or completes the first ('The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork', Ps 19:1). Learning to hear that echo is the key to reading the Psalms well.
40760: Headings give author, occasion, type (*mizmor*, a song with instruments; *maskil*, perhaps a teaching poem; *miktam*, uncertain), tune names ('according to The Doe of the Dawn', Ps 22) and directions 'to the choirmaster'. The word *Selah*, used 71 times, is probably a musical or liturgical marker, meaning uncertain.
40762: Laments complain directly to God ('How long, O LORD?'), ask for help, and usually turn to trust or a vow of praise. Complaint is permitted because the covenant binds God to his people; the psalmist holds God to his promises.
40764: Zion, the hill of the temple, is pictured as the centre of the world, the place of God's presence and protection. Pilgrims sang going up to the feasts.
40766: Some psalms celebrate the king, the LORD's 'anointed' (*mashiah*), at his coronation, wedding or battles. God calls him his 'son' (Ps 2:7), in the language of covenant adoption also found in 2 Sam 7:14. After the monarchy ended these psalms became prayers of hope for a coming King.
40768: Some psalms ask God to judge enemies harshly (Ps 109; Ps 137:8-9). They are prayers of victims who hand vengeance over to God rather than take it themselves, voiced in the strong idiom of the ancient world.
40770: Several psalms begin each line or stanza with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a way of saying 'everything from A to Z' and aiding memory. Ps 119 has 22 stanzas of 8 lines each.
40771:
The Psalms have shaped Jewish prayer more than any other book. A midrash on Ps 1 says that as Moses gave Israel the five books of the Torah, David gave Israel the five books of Psalms (Midrash Tehillim 1). The Mishnah lists the psalm the Levites sang for each day of the week in the temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4), and these are still said daily in synagogue, with Ps 92 for the Sabbath. Ps 145 (*Ashrei*) is said three times a day; Ps 145-150 form the core of the morning 'verses of song' (*Pesukei de-Zimra*); Ps 95-99 and Ps 29 welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening; and Ps 113-118, the *Hallel*, are sung at Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot and Hanukkah. At the Passover meal the Hallel is split around the meal, which is likely what Jesus and his disciples sang before going to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26). Ps 126 is sung before grace after meals on Sabbaths and festivals.

Outside the liturgy, saying the whole Psalter or chosen psalms is a traditional Jewish response to illness, danger and death; communities divide the 150 among themselves so the entire book is read for someone in need.

Read covenantally, the Psalms are the relationship between God and Israel spoken aloud. They praise the LORD's *hesed*, his loyal, covenant love (Ps 136 repeats 'for his hesed endures forever' 26 times), celebrate Torah as a delight rather than a burden (Ps 19:7-11; Ps 119), and give Israel permission to argue with God on the basis of his promises. Royal psalms, especially after the exile, were read as hopes for the Messiah, the son of David; the Targum and midrash apply several of them, such as Ps 2 and Ps 72, to the King Messiah.
40773: Ps 1 blesses those who meditate on Torah; Ps 2 enthrones the LORD's anointed over rebellious nations. Together they introduce the book.
40775: Mostly Davidic laments and trust psalms, from fleeing Absalom to quiet confidence in the Shepherd.
40777: Korahite psalms of longing for God's presence, David's confession, ending with a prayer for the ideal king.
40779: Asaph wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked and the ruined temple; Ps 89 asks why God has rejected David's line.
40781: Opening with Moses' prayer, it answers the crisis by looking past human kings to God's own kingship and the exodus story.
40783: Thanks for gathering the exiles, the Torah meditation of Ps 119, the pilgrim songs and the renewed hope of a Davidic king.
40785: Five psalms of pure praise end the book; everything that has breath is called to praise the LORD.
40814: The Hebrew title of the book, 'praises', from the same root as *hallelu-yah*, 'praise Yah'. Even the laments are gathered under this name.
40815: Loyal love that keeps covenant; kindness that goes beyond duty. It is the Psalter's most characteristic description of God.
40817: Teaching or instruction, not merely 'law'. The blessed person delights in it like a tree drinking from a stream.
40818: The king anointed with oil and adopted as God's 'son'; the source of the title Messiah (Greek *Christos*).
40820: To wait with expectant hope, like a cord stretched taut. Waiting for the LORD is active trust, not passivity.
40821: Several headings tie psalms to scenes in David's life, and Ps 18 appears almost word for word as 2 Sam 22.
40822: Chronicles describes David organising the temple singers and quotes psalm medleys at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem.
40823: Hebrews builds its argument for Jesus' sonship and priesthood on Ps 2, Ps 8, Ps 95 and Ps 110.
40824: Jesus quotes Ps 110 to ask how the Messiah can be David's son and Lord, and cries Ps 22:1 from the cross.
40825: Peter's first sermon reads Ps 16 and Ps 110 as fulfilled in the resurrection and ascension.
40826: Communal lament psalms such as Ps 74 and Ps 79 share the grief and language of Lamentations over the ruined temple.
40827: The Psalms are the Old Testament book most quoted in the New Testament. Jesus said that what was written about him 'in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms' must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The early church read the royal psalms as fulfilled in Jesus the anointed Son (Ps 2:7 in Acts 13:33; Ps 110:1 in Acts 2:34-35), and saw his passion in the laments he prayed (Ps 22; Ps 31:5 in Luke 23:46; Ps 69:9 in John 2:17). Jewish readers also look to the royal psalms for the coming Messiah but do not identify him with Jesus, and they read the laments primarily as the prayers of David and of Israel. Christians have often added a second insight: Jesus not only fulfils the Psalms but prays them, so those who pray the Psalms join their voice to his.
40829: Worship should be upbeat and victorious; complaint or anger toward God shows weak faith, so the lament and curse psalms are rarely sung or preached.
40830: About a third of the Psalms are laments, the largest single category. In the covenant relationship, bringing God your complaint is a sign of trust, not unbelief. Walter Brueggemann argued that churches which drop lament lose honesty and a sense of justice; Old Testament scholars broadly agree laments are central.
40831: Evangelical scholars such as Tremper Longman, Mark Vroegop and Carl Trueman (who asked 'What do miserable Christians sing?') have also urged churches to recover lament. They add, fairly, that most laments end in trust and praise, so the goal is honest movement toward God, not complaint for its own sake.
40832: Without lament, suffering people feel they must hide pain from God and from church. The Psalter gives them words that God himself put in Scripture.
40833: Reading individual verses as standalone promises
40834: Verses like 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart' (Ps 37:4) or 'no plague will come near your tent' (Ps 91:10) are personal guarantees that God will grant what I want or keep me from all harm.
40835: These lines are poetry within whole psalms. Ps 37 is a wisdom psalm urging patience while the wicked prosper, and the desires in view are shaped by delighting in God. Ps 91 expresses trust in God's protection; the devil himself quotes it to Jesus as a guarantee, and Jesus refuses to test God that way (Matt 4:6-7).
40836: Careful evangelical teachers agree, while insisting the psalms do give real comfort: God does protect and does give good gifts. The point is not to empty the promises but to read them as trust in a faithful God rather than as formulas.
40837: Formula readings set believers up for crushed faith when illness or loss comes; the psalms themselves include those very experiences.
